title: About
text:
I’m a data scientist who has spent six years inside elite football, first as a performance data analyst and now leading data insight for the Sport Science and Medical departments at Leicester City Football Club. My job is to turn large, messy performance data into information that coaches, practitioners and senior staff trust and act on.
I work across the whole data lifecycle: owning pipelines from external providers, building models, and designing self-serve tools so people can answer their own questions. I care as much about how an insight is communicated as about the analysis behind it.

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck
text:
Charts made in different tools drift apart. A ggplot in a report, a Shiny app and a slide deck each end up with their own colours and fonts, and colour starts to mean nothing in particular. The reader has to work out what to look at every time.
I wanted one set of rules that every output inherits automatically, so the design decisions are made once and the reader’s attention goes straight to the point.

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck
text:
Three words, turned into rules
The brand is built around three words: clear, analytical, sharp. Each one became a rule I could apply without thinking:

Clear: grey carries context and one colour carries the message. Every chart title states the answer, not the topic.
Analytical: colour has a job. Categorical, sequential, diverging and status colours are separate palettes, and none is borrowed for another’s purpose.
Sharp: one typeface (Inter), two weights, tabular numbers and no decoration that doesn’t carry information.

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck
text:
The palette









Slate gives structure, signal teal is the single accent, and a cool grey called context is used for everything that supports the message rather than being the message. Status colours are reserved for state (in range, monitor, out of range) and always appear with an icon or a word, never colour alone.

section: The core rule: grey for context, signal for the point
text:
The core rule: grey for context, signal for the point
The same data, drawn with default settings and then with the system. The default gives every player a different colour, so nothing stands out. With the system, the one player the chart is about is the only thing in colour, and the title says what the reader should take away.

BeforeAfter

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck
text:
Style as code
The rules live in one tokens file and are packaged for each tool I use, so a chart picks up the system with a line or two:
source("R/theme_md.R")

ggplot(df, aes(session, hsr, colour = player)) +
  geom_line() +
  md_highlight("Player 3") +   # grey for everyone except the focus
  theme_md()                   # type, gridlines, titles and captions
The same values drive a matplotlib and Plotly theme for Python, a Streamlit configuration, a Quarto slide theme, a PowerPoint template and this website.


1 source of truth for every colour and type style


6 tools that inherit it: R, Python, Streamlit, Quarto, PowerPoint, web


AA WCAG contrast for all text, in light and dark mode
